data.hypothesis: Increasing the large-path CTA tile from the previously measured 2048 inputs to 4096 should halve first-stage partials again (2048 to 1024 at n=4194304), retaining a separate direct-output final CTA and the existing modulo-based shared-memory reduction tree. This tests whether 1024 first-stage CTAs still provide enough parallelism while reducing partial traffic; total-run performance and full-domain correctness remain for controller evaluation.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use the 2048-input result as a comparison point, not proof that larger tiles will help; the CTA count and total-run timing must be measured for each tile.
memory_lessons.claim: The supplied T2 observations report valid results for both 1024- and 2048-input large-path tiles; the 2048-input trial measured faster (12.0186 μs) than the 1024-input trial (16.9348 μs), but do not establish that larger tiles are faster.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the 4096-input tile against both recorded trials under the full correctness and total-run timing protocol.

data.notes: The large-n route writes every first-stage partial before the following same-stream CTA reads them, and that CTA writes directly to out. The existing path for n <= 32768 is retained. The 4096-input candidate has not been measured; controller validation and total-run timing are required.
transformations: Add a large-path kernel that handles 4096 input values per CTA with 128 threads, accumulating 32 values per thread before using the existing modulo-based shared-memory reduction tree.
For n > 32768, launch ceil(n/4096) first-stage CTAs and one final CTA that reduces only the initialized partials and writes directly to out.
Leave the existing multi-stage reduction and copy path unchanged for n <= 32768.
